Writing a package that uses jlbind

Source: vignettes/writing-clients.qmd

This vignette explains how to add Julia functions to your own R package with jlbind. An R package that uses jlbind is called a client. jlbind compiles the Julia code of all installed clients into one shared library; see Get started with jlbind for how this works.

Set up

From your R package’s directory, run:

jlbind::use_jlbind()

This creates the files and configuration needed to connect the package to jlbind:

  • inst/julia/, containing a Julia binding package named after the R package with a Bindings suffix (for example, MyPkgBindings), including an example function.
  • src/jlbind.c and src/entrypoints.h, which register the native routines.
  • R/jlbind.R, which calls jlbind::bind() from .onLoad() and includes the roxygen tag for useDynLib().
  • The Config/jlbind and Imports: jlbind fields in DESCRIPTION.
  • A .jlbind/ directory for development builds, added to .Rbuildignore and .gitignore.

You can run use_jlbind() again safely. If your package already defines .onLoad(), add jlbind::bind(pkgname) to the existing function yourself. Then run devtools::document() to update NAMESPACE.

Important

Give the Julia binding package a unique name

All clients are compiled into the same library, so their Julia package names must not collide. Choose a binding package name that is unique among all R packages using jlbind, not just within your own R package.

That is why the default name is the R package name with a Bindings suffix.

Declare Julia functions

Inside the binding package, declare each function that R should be able to call using @rcall. Each declaration specifies the argument types and return type expected by the binding.

For example:

module MyPkgBindings

using JLBind

greet(name::String) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Union{Nothing,Float64}) =
    by === nothing ? x : x .+ by

@rcall greet(name::String)::String
@rcall shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Union{Nothing,Float64})::Vector{Float64}

end

The binding package is an ordinary Julia package. Declare its dependencies in Project.toml and import them as usual. In many cases, the actual computation lives in an existing Julia package, and the binding package only needs to declare the functions R should call and handle any necessary conversions.

Important

Write @rcall declarations literally at the top level

jlbind discovers @rcall declarations by scanning the Julia source files; it does not execute the module to find them. Keep the declarations at the top level of the module’s files rather than generating them dynamically or placing them inside functions or other runtime constructs.

Call them from R

Whenever you add or change @rcall declarations, regenerate the native routine list:

jlbind::update_entrypoints()

Each declared Julia function f becomes a native routine called C_f, which you can call from R using .Call():

greet <- function(name) .Call(C_greet, name)
shift <- function(x, by = NULL) .Call(C_shift, x, by)

The Julia side checks and converts the arguments, so the R wrappers can stay small. Use them to provide R-friendly defaults and documentation.

Build and test locally

During development, you usually want to build the library from your package’s source rather than from the installed clients. Run:

jlbind::build_library()
devtools::load_all()

By default, build_library() writes the library to .jlbind/ in your package’s source directory. That directory is excluded from the installed package. When you load the package with devtools::load_all(), jlbind uses this development library instead of the one created by install_backend().

Note

The development library is only used when your package loads first

The .jlbind/ library is selected only if your package is the first package using jlbind to be loaded in the R session. If another client has already loaded a different library, rebuilding your development library will not switch the active one. Restart R, then load your package first to test the new build.

If you need to use a library stored elsewhere, set the JLBIND_LIBRARY environment variable to its path before loading the package.

You can also test against an unreleased version of a Julia dependency by providing a local checkout through develop:

jlbind::build_library(develop = "~/dev/SomePackage.jl")
Tip

Pin the dependency versions

Include a Manifest.toml next to the binding package’s Project.toml with the Julia dependency versions known to compile with your package. CRAN’s policy asks that downloaded libraries be a fixed version rather than the latest.

Tests and CRAN

CRAN’s check machines do not have Julia installed, so your package must install and pass R CMD check without a compiled Julia library.

In tests, skip anything that needs the library:

skip_if_not(jlbind::is_bound("mypkg"))

In examples, wrap calls that require the library in if (jlbind::is_bound("mypkg")).

Types

@rcall converts each argument using from_sexp() and converts the return value using to_sexp(). The built-in conversions are:

Julia R argument R result
String, Symbol A single string A character vector of length one
Vector{String}, Vector{Symbol} A character vector A character vector
Float64 A single number A double
Int64 A single whole number A double
Int32 An integer
Bool TRUE or FALSE A logical
Vector{Float64}, Vector{Int64} A numeric vector A double vector
Vector{Int32} An integer vector
Vector{Bool} A logical vector A logical vector
Matrix{Float64} A double matrix
Union{Nothing,T} NULL, or a value of type T NULL, or a value of type T
Nothing NULL
Other Vectors, Tuples A list
NamedTuple A named list
RRef{T} A reference to a Julia object A reference to a Julia object
Vector{RRef{T}} A list of references

NA is an error wherever a value is expected. Likewise, an Int64 argument must be a whole number. Julia’s Int64 values become R doubles because R’s standard integers are only 32 bits; return Int32 if you need an R integer.

A binding package can support additional types by defining methods for JLBind.from_sexp(::Type{T}, x::SEXP) and JLBind.to_sexp(x::T). JLBind also provides helpers for building R objects directly, such as JLBind.data_frame(). See the JLBind source for the existing conversions and helpers.

Julia objects in R

Sometimes an object is easier to keep in Julia than to convert into an R data structure. You can pass such objects by reference using RRef{T}. R receives an external pointer to the Julia object, allowing it to be reused across calls. The object is released when R garbage-collects the reference.

For example, define a mutable Julia object and expose functions that operate on it:

mutable struct Counter
    n::Int64
end

JLBind.r_class(::Type{Counter}) = "counter"

new_counter(start::Int64) = Counter(start)
increment(c::Counter, by::Int64) = (c.n += by; c.n)

@rcall new_counter(start::Int64)::RRef{Counter}
@rcall increment(c::RRef{Counter}, by::Int64)::Int64

From R, you can create a counter and update it across calls:

counter <- new_counter(0)
class(counter)
#> [1] "counter"

increment(counter, 2)
#> [1] 2

r_class() sets the R class of the external pointer, so your package can define methods such as print() for it. An argument declared as RRef{Counter} also checks that the reference points to a Counter, rather than accepting an arbitrary Julia object.

Errors

If a function called through @rcall throws a Julia exception, jlbind turns it into an R error. The messages from ArgumentError, ErrorException, DimensionMismatch, OverflowError, and AssertionError are passed through. Other exceptions are summarized.

fail(msg::String) = throw(ArgumentError(msg))
@rcall fail(msg::String)::Nothing

Calling the function from R then produces an ordinary R error:

fail("bad input")
#> Error: bad input

The same principle applies to argument conversion: if an R value has the wrong type or cannot be converted to the requested Julia type, jlbind reports an error rather than allowing an invalid value through.

Compilation constraints (trimming)

By default, jlbind compiles the shared library with juliac --trim=safe. This keeps the compiled image small by including only code reachable from the functions exposed through @rcall. It also requires calls to be resolvable at compile time.

If your package cannot be compiled with trimming, add the following field to DESCRIPTION:

Config/jlbind/trim: false

This disables trimming and allows code that cannot be resolved ahead of time to compile.

Warning

An untrimmed library includes the full Julia system image and is much larger, so avoid it if you can.

Abstract types

With trimming, a common source of compilation errors is a function that accepts several concrete types through an abstract RRef. Suppose your binding package works with shapes:

abstract type Shape end

struct Circle <: Shape
    radius::Float64
end
struct Square <: Shape
    side::Float64
end
struct Rectangle <: Shape
    width::Float64
    height::Float64
end
struct Triangle <: Shape
    base::Float64
    height::Float64
end

JLBind.r_class(::Type{<:Shape}) = "shape"

area(s::Circle) = pi * s.radius^2
area(s::Square) = s.side^2
area(s::Rectangle) = s.width * s.height
area(s::Triangle) = s.base * s.height / 2

An entrypoint that takes an RRef{Shape} knows only that its argument is some Shape. If it simply calls area(s), the compiler cannot tell which of the four methods that call reaches, and the build fails with an error such as:

Verifier error #1: unresolved call from statement area(s::Shape)::Any

One possible solution is to branch on the concrete types once, with @nospecialize, and to make the call inside each branch, where the type is known:

function with_shape(f::F, @nospecialize(s::Shape)) where {F}
    s isa Circle && return f(s)
    s isa Square && return f(s)
    s isa Rectangle && return f(s)
    s isa Triangle && return f(s)
    throw(ArgumentError("unknown shape"))
end

circle(radius::Float64) = Circle(radius)
square(side::Float64) = Square(side)
rectangle(width::Float64, height::Float64) = Rectangle(width, height)
triangle(base::Float64, height::Float64) = Triangle(base, height)
shape_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape)) = with_shape(area, s)
scaled_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape), factor::Float64) =
    with_shape(x -> factor^2 * area(x), s)

@rcall circle(radius::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall square(side::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall rectangle(width::Float64, height::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall triangle(base::Float64, height::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall shape_area(s::RRef{Shape})::Float64
@rcall scaled_area(s::RRef{Shape}, factor::Float64)::Float64

With the R wrappers

circle <- function(radius) .Call(C_circle, radius)
square <- function(side) .Call(C_square, side)
rectangle <- function(width, height) .Call(C_rectangle, width, height)
triangle <- function(base, height) .Call(C_triangle, base, height)
shape_area <- function(shape) .Call(C_shape_area, shape)
scaled_area <- function(shape, factor) .Call(C_scaled_area, shape, factor)

every shape can be passed to the same functions:

shapes <- list(circle(1), square(2), rectangle(2, 3), triangle(2, 3))
vapply(shapes, shape_area, numeric(1))
#> [1] 3.141593 4.000000 6.000000 3.000000

scaled_area(square(2), 3)
#> [1] 36

Without a @nospecialize on with_shape Julia will compile a separate copy of with_shape for each concrete shape, and the call into it cannot be resolved for the same reason as area(s). Functions that pass the shape on to with_shape, such as shape_area, should also take it with @nospecialize. Small functions like these are inlined, so this example would compile without it, but larger ones fail the same way.

If a hierarchy has only a few types, some alternatives to @nospecialize are:

  • Declare a separate entrypoint for each concrete type (RRef{Circle},RRef{Square}, …) and choose between them in R.

  • Use a small Union such as RRef{Union{Circle,Square}}, which Julia resolves by checking each member in turn.
